segments.text: Neural networks require numbers, so a text pipeline must turn symbols into usable numerical representations.
Tokenization divides text into units, such as words, subwords or characters.
A vocabulary assigns each token an integer ID. Larger IDs do not mean larger or more important meanings.
A one-hot vector marks one vocabulary position with one and all others with zero. It encodes identity but no built-in semantic similarity.
A large vocabulary makes these identity vectors wide and sparse.
An embedding table stores a shorter, dense vector for each token ID.
Looking up an ID selects its row. The embedding values are learned parameters that can receive gradients during training.
A prediction task supplies a learning signal. Tokens used in similar ways can develop useful relationships in the learned space.
A two-dimensional plot is a simplified view of vectors that usually have many more coordinates.
Nearby vectors may reflect useful similarities. Individual dimensions need not correspond to human-readable concepts.
Vector arithmetic can illustrate relationships, but analogy patterns depend on the training data and objective.
Cosine similarity compares directions: dot product divided by the product of vector lengths. Values range from minus one to one for nonzero vectors.
Aligned directions have cosine one; perpendicular directions have cosine zero. Opposite directions have cosine minus one, without guaranteeing opposite meanings.
Averaging token vectors produces a simple text representation but discards token order.
Static lookup gives a token the same starting vector in different sentences. Contextual models update its representation using surrounding information.
